title: Ginger infusion for morning sickness
subtitle: A low-dose ginger tea for pregnancy nausea
excerpt: A mild infusion of dried ginger root in hot water for pregnancy-related nausea. Ginger at low dose is one of the few herbal remedies with limited clinical-trial evidence for use in the first trimester. The dose limit is important: no more than 1 g dried ginger per cup, no more than four cups a day. Readers with a high-risk pregnancy, history of miscarriage, or any bleeding should consult their midwife before starting.

content.text: Ginger infusion for morning sickness is a mild cup of dried ginger root steeped in hot water, drunk in small amounts throughout the day during pregnancy-related nausea. Ginger is one of the few herbal remedies with limited clinical-trial evidence supporting its use for nausea in early pregnancy at low doses. The dose limit is the central safety point of this entry: no more than half a teaspoon of dried ginger per cup (around 1 g), and no more than four cups a day. This keeps intake within the range the available evidence covers. More than this has not been studied in pregnancy and sits in the cautious column.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms. Dose limits matter here: do not exceed half a teaspoon of dried ginger per cup (approximately 1 g), and do not drink more than four cups a day. Higher doses have not been studied in pregnancy and are in the cautious column. Readers with a high-risk pregnancy, a history of miscarriage, any bleeding in this pregnancy, or any pregnancy complication should consult their midwife or doctor before starting ginger tea. Drug interactions: ginger has mild antiplatelet activity. Readers on warfarin, aspirin, or other anticoagulants should keep ginger to culinary levels and discuss therapeutic doses with their prescriber. Anticoagulants should not be combined with therapeutic ginger without medical supervision.

attrs.title: Fresh ginger is an alternative
attrs.body: A thin slice of fresh ginger root (about 5 g) can replace the dried ground ginger. Fresh ginger is generally milder and is a useful option for those who find the ground ginger too sharp. Peel a thin slice, add it to the cup with the hot water, steep covered for ten minutes, and remove before drinking.

content.text: Measure half a teaspoon of dried ground ginger into a cup or teapot.
Pour over just-off-the-boil water. Cover with a lid or saucer.
Stir well, add honey if using, and strain into a cup if you used loose dried ginger. Sip slowly while warm.

One cup at a time, sipped slowly, up to a maximum of four cups in a day. This keeps total dried ginger intake at or below 4 g per day, which is the limit the available evidence on pregnancy safety covers. Do not exceed this. Limited clinical-trial evidence supports ginger at low doses for pregnancy nausea; the evidence covers the first trimester. When not to use this remedy

Do not exceed the dose limits above. Do not use this remedy if you are on warfarin, aspirin, or other anticoagulants without first discussing it with your prescriber. Stop and see your midwife or doctor if nausea is accompanied by severe vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, signs of dehydration (dark urine, dizziness, confusion), or any bleeding. Nausea that is severe or persistent needs a midwife or GP assessment, not just a home remedy.
